title: Born of tapas
hookLine: the power goes out on a night with no moon. In the creation hymn's dark, the One is born of tapas, heat: why Hindus fast and keep vows
carry: tapas: the holy heat of discipline
tomorrow: which comes first, a thought or a want?

lines: EYES OPEN, EYES SHUT: THE SAME.
cards: The power goes out on a night with no moon. You shut your eyes, then open them, and can't tell the difference. The dark behind your eyelids and the dark of the room have become one dark.

Your hand is somewhere in front of your face, but you couldn't prove it. Nothing has an edge. The Nasadiya Sukta's third verse begins in that kind of dark, and pushes it further than any power cut could.

teach.b: In Sanskrit the verse opens tama asit tamasa gulham agre. Darkness there was, hidden by darkness, in the beginning. Not darkness covering something: darkness covering darkness.
Nothing to see, and nothing to see it with.

teach.h: WATER WITH NO MARK ON IT.
teach.b: In paraphrase it goes on: all this was water, with no mark on it, nothing told apart from anything else.
That's the hymn's picture of the start: not an empty space with sharp edges, but a sameness so complete that nothing could stand out. Then the turn.

teach.h: THE ONE, BORN BY THE POWER OF TAPAS.
teach.b: What was coming into being lay covered by emptiness, and that One was born by the power of tapas.
Tapas is a word for heat.

teach.h: TAPAS: THE HOLY HEAT OF DISCIPLINE.
teach.b: And here's the part to tell a friend tonight: the same word names the heat a person builds through vows, fasting and long prayer. Notice what the verse leaves out.
It doesn't say who made the heat, or name a god striking a spark. First, sameness, dark on dark. Then warmth.
Then one thing that could be told apart. Later texts take the thread further. The Taittiriya Upanishad says the One wished to become many, performed tapas, and having done it, made all this.
So when a grandmother fasts on Ekadashi, or a family keeps a vow through a festival, the tradition doesn't see mere going without.
It sees tapas: the same warm power the world was born from, building in a person, and offered to God.

how: Many Hindus keep vratas, vows, and fasts such as Ekadashi, understood as tapas: a discipline offered to God. The Nasadiya Sukta itself is kept in traditional recitation, learned by memory from a teacher.

o: the hymn of creation: dark on dark, then heat
a spell that keeps the darkness away
a hymn for lighting the lamps at nightfall

games.q: the third verse — tap the pairs.
p: water with no mark on it
born by the power of heat

s: the third verse names the god who lit the fire
it says the One was born by the power of tapas, heat, and names no maker.
in the verse, darkness is hidden by darkness
tama asit tamasa gulham agre: darkness there was, hidden by darkness, in the beginning.
the verse pictures the start as empty space with sharp edges
it pictures water with no mark on it, nothing told apart from anything else.

games.q: you're the poet. everything is dark and the same. what brings the first one thing into being?
games.why: the third verse says the One was born by the power of tapas, heat. it doesn't say where the heat came from.

practice: Choose one small vow for today, the way families keep a vrata: one meal kept simple, no phone for the first hour, or one kind thing done without being thanked.

Then close your eyes or lower your gaze, let the dark be plain, and find one warm place, the hands resting together or the middle of the chest. Rest there, holding the vow, coming back whenever a thought pulls you off.
If you pray, offer the vow to God; if not, keep it for someone you love.

wordCard.voice: The Nasadiya Sukta. The hymn of creation. In its third verse, darkness hidden by darkness, until the One was born by the power of heat.

orig.note: Sanskrit: heat. In Rig Veda 10.129.3 the One is born by its power; later texts also use it for the heat of discipline.

carryVoice: Your line: tapas, the holy heat of discipline. First dark on dark, then warmth. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 10.129.3 (all this was undistinguished water; what was coming to be was covered by the void; that One was born by the power of tapas)
Taittiriya Upanishad 2.6 (he desired: may I be many; he performed tapas; having performed tapas, he created all this)
